prompt: In reserve.py, why did move_hold leave Bia with no place in the queue?

choices.text: The foreign key deleted her hold when the insert named a member who does not exist
choices.why: A foreign key refuses the bad row; it deleted nothing. The delete was the program's own statement.

choices.text: The delete was committed before the insert failed
choices.why: Right. With no transaction around them, each statement is committed on its own, so the failure could only undo itself.

choices.text: SQLite does not support transactions in a database held in memory
choices.why: It does: move_hold_atomically ran against the same kind of database and rolled back.

choices.text: The CHECK on place refused her place number
choices.why: Her place was 1, which the CHECK accepts; the error printed was about the foreign key.

prompt: Match each ACID letter to where the section finds it, or misses it, in reserve.py.

pairs.right: absent, because the database lives in memory
not shown until the next section

prompt: A Go function calls db.Exec("BEGIN"), then the delete and the insert, then db.Exec("COMMIT"), all on a *sql.DB. What is wrong?

choices.text: Nothing; database/sql notices the BEGIN and keeps the following calls inside it
choices.why: It does not parse your SQL; it hands each call whatever connection the pool has free.

choices.text: Each call gets whichever pooled connection is free, outside the transaction
choices.why: Right. A transaction belongs to one connection, which is why BeginTx returns a Tx to run the statements on.

choices.text: Go has no way to run BEGIN as SQL
choices.why: Exec will send it; the problem is which connection receives it and which receives the next call.

prompt: The first run of desks.py ends with available=0 and loans=2. What happened?

choices.text: Desk B wrote a count worked out from a value desk A had already changed
choices.why: Right. Both read 1 and both wrote 1 - 1; the second write replaced the first. That is the lost update.

choices.text: SQLite dropped desk A's UPDATE because two connections wrote at once
choices.why: Both UPDATEs ran in turn, in one thread. Nothing was dropped; desk B simply wrote the same 0.

choices.text: An insert into loans failed silently
choices.why: Both inserts succeeded; that is why there are two loans.

prompt: Three desks follow the no_transaction pattern on a title with 2 copies: all three read first, then each writes seen - 1 and records a loan. What does available say at the end?
hint: Every desk saw the same number.

prompt: The lend of desks.py, read then write, runs inside one transaction on a PostgreSQL left at its default level. Two desks overlap. What happens?

choices.text: The second desk gets database is locked, as in the plain_begin run
choices.why: That is SQLite, which is serializable. PostgreSQL defaults to read committed.

choices.text: PostgreSQL aborts the second transaction with a serialization error
choices.why: That needs REPEATABLE READ or higher; the default level lets the second UPDATE through.

choices.text: The update is lost, unless the read says FOR UPDATE
choices.why: Right. Read committed waits for the first UPDATE and then applies the second over it.

choices.text: Nothing goes wrong: any transaction serialises its own reads and writes
choices.why: A transaction groups its own statements; whether it is shielded from another one is the isolation level's business.

prompt: Caio's first visit in uow.py calls uow.lend and leaves the with block. Why is nothing written?

choices.text: SQLite refused the loan because the basket held a single title
choices.why: No SQL ran at all: lend only appends to a list.

choices.text: Only commit writes, and __exit__ throws away what was never committed
choices.why: Right. Forgetting commit writes nothing, which is the safe way round to forget.

choices.text: Dom Casmurro had no copy left by then
choices.why: The stock still showed 2 after Bia's refused basket.

prompt: Put in order what happens inside commit for Bia's basket of Dom Casmurro, Vidas Secas and Iracema.
items: BEGIN IMMEDIATE takes the write lock
Dom Casmurro and Vidas Secas are counted down and their loans inserted
The UPDATE for Iracema changes zero rows
ROLLBACK undoes the two loans already applied
trap: The first two loans do reach the database inside the transaction; the rollback is what keeps them from being seen.

prompt: Instead of a unit of work, checkout calls a lend_one helper that commits after each title. Bia asks for three titles and the third has no copy. What does she leave with?

choices.text: Nothing, because the error rolls the whole checkout back
choices.why: There is nothing left to roll back: each of the first two was committed when lend_one finished.

choices.text: The first two titles
choices.why: Right. Each commit ended its own transaction, so the basket was lent in pieces.

choices.text: All three, with the stock of the third going below zero
choices.why: The conditional UPDATE refuses when no copy is left; that part still works.

choices.text: Only the third, which the database kept as the latest change
choices.why: The third is the one that failed; it is the only title she cannot have.

prompt: In the CP run of branches.py, the link is down. Why does Centro still lend the copy to Bia?

choices.text: It is the primary, so its count is the truth
choices.why: Right. CP refuses on the side that cannot be sure, and the primary can be.

choices.text: CP mode only refuses after the link has been down for some time
choices.why: There is no timer in the program; Vila Madalena refuses at once.

choices.text: Bia asked first, and the first request in a partition is always accepted
choices.why: Order is not the rule. Had Caio asked at Vila Madalena first, he would still have been refused.

prompt: Somebody sums up CAP as "pick two of the three". What does the section say is wrong with that?

choices.text: There are four properties, not three
choices.why: CAP has three letters; the misreading is about what choosing means.

choices.text: Every real system must give up availability
choices.why: The AP run gives up consistency instead; both answers exist.

choices.text: A partition is not optional; the choice exists only while one is happening
choices.why: Right. You cannot choose to skip partitions, so the real choice is what each side does during one.

choices.text: It is right, but only for databases with more than two nodes
choices.why: The library has two branches and the choice is just as real there.

prompt: The literature's name for CAP's C, every read seeing the most recent write as if there were one copy, is ___ .
In latency.py, ONE_WAY_MS is changed to 80 and LOCAL_MS stays 3. How long does Bia wait in sync mode, in milliseconds?
hint: The confirmation has to come back as well.

prompt: In the async run, a read from the replica at 40 ms says 16 March. What is that?

choices.text: A partition: the replica cannot be reached
choices.why: Nothing is broken in the program; the change is simply still on its way.

choices.text: Eventual consistency: a stale read with no failure anywhere
choices.why: Right. It is the everyday price of telling Bia "done" after 3 ms.

choices.text: A lost update, like the first run of desks.py
choices.why: Nothing was overwritten: at 80 ms the replica shows 30 March.

choices.text: A bug in the replica, which should have applied the change first
choices.why: The replica cannot have a change that has not reached it; 55 ms of travel is the design.

prompt: A store answers reads from the nearest replica when the network is healthy, and refuses writes on the side cut off from the primary during a partition. Which PACELC label fits?

choices.text: PA/EL
choices.why: Refusing on the cut-off side is choosing C during a partition, not A.

choices.text: PC/EL
choices.why: Right. C when partitioned, latency otherwise: the two halves of the tree are chosen separately.

choices.text: PC/EC
choices.why: Answering from the nearest replica, without waiting, is the L side of Else.

choices.text: PA/EC
choices.why: Both halves are the other way round.

prompt: Which library operation does the section accept at any branch while the link is down?

choices.text: Lending the last copy, as long as each branch keeps a record
choices.why: Keeping a record is what led to two loans for one copy in the AP run.

choices.text: Placing a hold
choices.why: Right. A queue ordered by arrival time settles the conflict by rule, without a person.

choices.text: Paying a fine, since the amount is known in advance
choices.why: Money taken twice needs a refund, which is a person repairing it; fines go to the primary.

prompt: Which of these operations does the section send to the primary and pay for consistency? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: Lending the last copy
choices.why: Right. Two members promised one book is a mistake a person has to repair.

choices.text: Showing "available" in the online catalogue
choices.why: A few seconds stale harms nobody; it reads from a replica or lesson 8's read model.

choices.text: Paying a fine
choices.why: Right. Money, and every ACID letter with it.

choices.text: Counting "popular this week"
choices.why: A count off by a few is harmless; the section gives it no transaction at all.

prompt: A new operation: a member rates a book from 1 to 5, and the page shows the average. The link between branches goes down. What does the section's test suggest?

choices.text: Accept at both branches and merge the ratings when the link returns
choices.why: Right. Every rating counts once whichever branch heard it, so a rule settles it and nobody has to be phoned.

choices.text: Refuse at Vila Madalena, as for lending the last copy
choices.why: Lending is refused because only a person can repair two loans for one copy; two ratings conflict with nothing.

choices.text: Run every rating inside BEGIN IMMEDIATE at the primary, so no rating is lost
choices.why: That buys consistency nobody needs and makes every rating wait behind the loans.

prompt: Each branch in the AP run has data that satisfies every constraint, yet the two disagree. Which statement is true?

choices.text: The run breaks ACID, because two loans exist for one copy
choices.why: Each branch's own transactions were valid; no single database broke a rule it was given.

choices.text: Both Cs fail, since they are the same property seen from two sides
choices.why: They are different properties; the section tables them apart for this reason.

choices.text: ACID's C holds on each node; CAP's C fails between them
choices.why: Right. Valid data per node, and copies that disagree: the two letters measure different things.

choices.text: Neither C applies, because the network was down
choices.why: A partition is exactly when CAP's C is decided, and ACID applies on each node regardless.

prompt: The online catalogue reads "available: 1" from a replica. A member sees it, walks to the desk, and the copy has just gone out. What should the library do about it?

choices.text: Move the catalogue to synchronous reads from the primary
choices.why: Even a current page goes stale the moment the member stands up; the cost would buy nothing at the desk.

choices.text: Nothing: the page traded consistency for latency, and the desk still checks at the primary
choices.why: Right. The lend itself is where consistency is paid for, and it refused correctly.

choices.text: Treat it as a lost update and add BEGIN IMMEDIATE to the page
choices.why: Nothing was overwritten; a read was simply old. A lock on a read path would make every page view queue.

choices.text: Hold the copy for anyone who has the page open
choices.why: That turns every page view into a write at the primary, the most expensive choice in the table.
